subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Behind the fun theme sit three solid computing ideas. The first is inputs and outputs. An input is data that goes into a computer (a key press, a click, a sound at the microphone), and the hardware that sends it in is an input device. An output is information the computer sends back out to us (a picture on the screen, a sound from the speaker), and the hardware that carries it out is an output device. The headline objective of the whole unit is to build a program that produces different outputs from different inputs — press one key and something happy happens, press another and something different happens. The second idea is decomposition — breaking a big problem into smaller parts. When our badge has to do two different things, decomposition tells us we actually need two separate algorithms, one for each job. The third idea is writing and reading algorithms: setting out the steps in order (we use a simple table), predicting what an algorithm will do before we run it, and picking out its components (what starts it, what it shows, how long for, and how many times it repeats).

outcomes: Explain what an input is and what an output is, in their own words.
Identify common input devices (keyboard, mouse, microphone, touchscreen, camera) and output devices (screen, speaker, headphones, printer).
Explain that our five senses are the body's own input devices.
Use decomposition to break a problem into smaller parts, and explain why a badge that does two jobs needs two algorithms.
Write an algorithm as an ordered list of steps, and predict its outcome before running it.
Identify the components of an algorithm: what starts it, what it shows, how long for, and how many times it repeats.
Build a program in Scratch that produces different outputs from different inputs, using an event block such as when [a] key pressed.
Reuse repetition (the repeat ( ) loop) to make an output happen a set number of times, and add a comment to explain the code.

Before this unit (from the syllabus), children should already use logical thinking to create algorithms, follow and correct algorithms that use repetition, understand that decomposition means breaking a task into parts, and create a simple program that produces an output from an input. A quick recap of the repeat block at the start of Session 3 is usually enough.

concepts.title: Inputs and outputs all around us (unplugged)
concepts.explanation: A computer takes in inputs and gives back outputs. An input is data going in; an output is information coming out. The hardware that carries data in is an input device (keyboard, mouse, microphone, touchscreen, camera); the hardware that carries information out is an output device (screen, speaker, headphones, printer). You have five amazing input devices of your own — your senses. Your eyes take in sight, your ears take in sound, your nose takes in smell, your tongue takes in taste, your skin takes in touch.
concepts.example: They send information into your brain, the way a keyboard sends letters into a computer. Input in, output out.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you name two input devices and two output devices? Can you see that the senses are inputs?

concepts.title: Decomposition and algorithms (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
Decomposition means breaking a big problem into smaller parts so each part is easy to solve. An algorithm is a set of steps in the right order to do a job. When we plan a gadget, we first decompose it into its separate jobs, then write one algorithm for each job.

Each small part is its own little list of steps. Breaking a big job into smaller parts is called decomposition. Our badge must do two things. When you press the a key it shows a happy face and a happy sound.
concepts.example: When you press the b key it shows a sad face and a different sound. Is that one job or two?
concepts.checkYourself: Can you see that two jobs need two algorithms?

concepts.title: Different input, different output (Scratch)
concepts.explanation: Now we build for real. In Scratch, a script starts with an event block — a “hat” block that waits for an input. when [a] key pressed waits for the a key (our input); the blocks under it are the output. Name the three parts of the screen in child words: the coloured blocks on the left, the script area where we join them, and the stage with the cat sprite. The cat already has a sound called Meow. First recap repeat from earlier in the year, then build this together and try it by pressing the a key
concepts.example: Find one real example of different input, different output (Scratch) around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you drop blocks inside the repeat loop (not underneath it)? Can you start a script with an event block?

concepts.title: Two algorithms in one program (Scratch)
concepts.explanation: A real gadget does more than one thing, so it needs more than one algorithm — this is decomposition in action. Today we add a second script, started by a different input (the b key), giving a different output. Now the same program produces different outputs from different inputs, which is the headline objective of the unit. Add a second, separate script in the same script area (scripts can sit side by side and do not touch). Build the sad badge together, and notice on purpose that it repeats a different number of times and shows for a different length Keep the happy badge from Session 3.
concepts.example: Find one real example of two algorithms in one program (Scratch) around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you connect the two side-by-side scripts back to the word decomposition? Can you build a second, separate script started by a different key?

concepts.title: Be an innovator: invent your own gadget (Scratch)
concepts.explanation: This session flows straight into the Mini-Project. Talk about inventors for a minute: an innovator sees a problem and builds something useful to solve it. Clicking the sprite is another kind of input — the mouse is an input device too Ask what small gadget could help at Ehel Academy or at home — a badge that reminds you when it is time to tidy up, a helper that greets a visitor, a quiet-please signal for the library. Then show how to add a third input using the mouse.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: be an innovator: invent your own gadget (Scratch). Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you add a third input with its own output? Can you plan with an algorithm before building?

workedExamples.title: Worked example 4: Two algorithms in one program (Scratch)
workedExamples.prompt: Predict. Script A does repeat (5) and shows a face for 1 second each time. Script B does repeat (2) and shows a face for 3 seconds each time. Which script runs for longer?
workedExamples.solution: Script A = 5 x 1 = 5 seconds; Script B = 2 x 3 = 6 seconds. Script B runs for longer (more repeats does not always mean more time).

debugging.symptom: More repeats always take more time.

selfAssessment: I can explain what an input is and what an output is, in their own words.
I can identify common input devices (keyboard, mouse, microphone, touchscreen, camera) and output devices (screen, speaker, headphones, printer).
I can explain that our five senses are the body's own input devices.
I can use decomposition to break a problem into smaller parts, and explain why a badge that does two jobs needs two algorithms.
I can write an algorithm as an ordered list of steps, and predict its outcome before running it.
I can identify the components of an algorithm: what starts it, what it shows, how long for, and how many times it repeats.
I can build a program in Scratch that produces different outputs from different inputs, using an event block such as when [a] key pressed.
I can reuse repetition (the repeat ( ) loop) to make an output happen a set number of times, and add a comment to explain the code.

I can before this unit (from the syllabus), children should already use logical thinking to create algorithms, follow and correct algorithms that use repetition, understand that decomposition means breaking a task into parts, and create a simple program that produces an output from an input. A quick recap of the repeat block at the start of Session 3 is usually enough.
